TextView.android:text: Required to read GnssStatus & NavIC signals
NavIC satellites remain high overhead India 24/7/365, shining signals down dense urban street canyons without skyscraper obstruction.
Listening for IRNSS L5 & S-band signals...
Whenever people casually say "turn on GPS", your phone is actually using GNSS. GNSS is the scientific umbrella term for all space-based positioning networks orbiting Earth.

Just as in India we say "Bisleri" for packaged water, "Surf" for detergent, or "Colgate" for toothpaste, people casually say "GPS" for satellite location. But GPS (NAVSTAR) is only America's military system. Your smartphone combines 6 international constellations simultaneously.
The 6 GNSS Constellations in Your Phone:

• NavIC [IND] (India / ISRO) — 10 Regional Satellites in Orbit (GEO/GSO)
• GPS [USA] (USA / Space Force) — 31 Global MEO Satellites
• Galileo [EUR] (Europe / ESA) — 26 High-Precision Satellites
• BeiDou [CHN] (China / CNSA) — 45 Multi-Orbit Satellites
• GLONASS [RUS] (Russia / Roscosmos) — 24 Satellites
• QZSS [JPN] (Japan / JAXA) — 4 Asia-Pacific Satellites
All satellites broadcast on the same carrier frequency (like NavIC L5 on 1176.45 MHz). To avoid radio collision, each satellite transmits a unique orthogonal binary code (PRN).

Your phone's baseband matches this mathematical sequence using Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA). To standard radio scanners it sounds like static "Noise", but because it is pre-programmed, it is "Pseudo-Random".
NavIC PRN Codes: PRN 01 (1A), PRN 02 (1B), PRN 03 (1C), PRN 05 (1E), PRN 06 (1F), PRN 07 (1G), PRN 09 (1I), PRN 10 (NVS-01), PRN 11 (NVS-02), PRN 12 (NVS-03 Gen-2).

In dense Indian metropolises like Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Delhi, tall high-rises block foreign GPS satellites orbiting low near the horizon (30°–40° elevation). Signals reflect off concrete, creating severe multipath position drift.
NavIC satellites, however, are stationed near Zenith (70°–85° high elevation directly overhead). Like the midday sun, their radio waves shine straight down street canyons without building blockage!

Unlike American GPS satellites that race across the sky at 3.9 km/s and set every few hours, ISRO stationed NavIC at 35,786 km in synchronous orbits:

• 3 Geostationary (GEO): Positioned directly above the equator at 83°E, 32.5°E, and 129.5°E. From India they appear completely motionless in the sky 24/7/365.

• 7 Geosynchronous (GSO): Inclined at 29°, tracing an analemma (figure-8) over 55°E and 111.75°E for high-elevation geometry.

• NVS Second-Gen (NVS-01, NVS-02, NVS-03): Feature indigenous space-grade Rubidium atomic clocks and add the L1 civilian frequency.

01. Dual-Band RF Antenna: Tunes into L1 (1575 MHz) and L5 (1176 MHz). Comparing both frequencies cancels ionospheric atmospheric delay.

02. Baseband Correlators: Aligns PRN code sequences to calculate nanosecond travel time from atomic clocks in orbit.

03. Trilateration Engine: Solves equations for 3D coordinates (X, Y, Z) and receiver clock offset. Modern phones fuse 30+ satellites.

04. A-GNSS Over 4G/5G: Cellular towers push orbit ephemeris in 1s, slashing time-to-first-fix from 45s down to 1.5s.

05. IMU Sensor Fusion: An Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) fuses satellite fixes with accelerometer, gyro, and barometer for tunnels and flyovers.
